questions.q: What is the core problem with pasting an API key or connection string directly into application code?
options: It makes the code run slower
It ends up in source control, logs, and screen shares as a standing liability that's hard to fully remove
Azure refuses to run code containing secrets
It only works in development environments, never production
questions.explain: A hardcoded secret spreads wherever the code goes — version control history, logs, backups — and is difficult to ever fully revoke.

questions.q: What does enabling a system-assigned managed identity on a VM actually require from the developer?
options: Generating and securely storing a new client secret
A single checkbox at resource creation — no secret is issued to anyone
Manually rotating a password every 90 days
Writing custom authentication code from scratch
questions.explain: A system-assigned managed identity is enabled with one checkbox, and Azure manages the underlying credential — there's no secret for a developer to handle.

questions.q: Where does a managed identity actually get registered, and how do you confirm it's really on?
options: In Microsoft Entra ID, confirmed via the resource's own Identity blade showing Status: On
It isn't registered anywhere — it's purely cosmetic
In the Azure Resource Manager template file only
In a local .env file on the VM
questions.explain: A managed identity is a real identity in Microsoft Entra ID, and the resource's Identity blade is where you confirm its status.

questions.q: If a VM has a managed identity enabled, can it automatically read secrets from any Key Vault?
options: Yes, managed identities have access to every Key Vault in the subscription by default
No — access must still be granted explicitly, through an access policy or RBAC role naming that identity
Only if the VM and Key Vault are in the same resource group
Only if the Key Vault's public access is enabled
questions.explain: An identity existing doesn't grant access to anything — explicit permission still has to be assigned to that identity on the target resource.

questions.q: What actually changes in application code when switching from `ClientSecretCredential` to `DefaultAzureCredential`?
options: The SDK call is completely rewritten and the client class changes entirely
The credential object changes, removing the need for a client secret anywhere in code, config, or environment variables
The application must switch programming languages
Nothing changes — both require an identical client secret
questions.explain: The SDK call (like SecretClient) stays the same; only the credential object changes, and DefaultAzureCredential picks up the managed identity with no secret required.
